scenario: A reusable metadata-validation CLI must run on developer machines and CI. The current metadata needs only top-level scalars and lists, but future extensibility is plausible. The team wants one supported local-and-CI path.
question: Which dependency strategy did this project adopt for v0.1?

choices.A: Use one Python-standard-library CLI and deliberately keep the supported metadata grammar narrow.
choices.B: Use one Python CLI with a reviewed external YAML package so full YAML semantics are available from the start.
choices.C: Use a shell-based local initializer and a separate Python CI validator optimized for each environment.
choices.D: Use a Node.js CLI with a schema package and wrap it separately for CI.

scenario: A reusable toolkit updates files it manages in adopter repositories. Adopters may edit those managed files locally, while project-owned configuration, records, documentation, rules, and CI remain outside toolkit ownership.
question: Which conflict policy did this project adopt for upgrades?

choices.A: Back up toolkit-managed files and overwrite them from the new release, leaving project-owned files untouched.
choices.B: Treat the entire toolkit directory as package-owned and replace it atomically during upgrades.
choices.C: Use best-effort three-way merge, continue updating cleanly merged files, and surface unresolved conflicts.
choices.D: Track toolkit-managed files by hash, support dry-run, and abort all writes if any managed file differs from its recorded hash.

scenario: An automation workflow generates translated documentation and all configured structural and terminology checks pass. The generated text may still contain semantic or stylistic issues outside those machine checks.
question: Which publication boundary did this project adopt?

choices.A: Produce review artifacts and require a human-reviewed publication change; the generation workflow itself does not publish.
choices.B: Open a draft pull request automatically but always require a human merge before publication.
choices.C: Publish automatically when all configured structural and terminology gates pass.
choices.D: Publish automatically only when the machine gates pass and the translator also reports high confidence.

scenario: A reusable AI-backed workflow is being stabilized. Multiple providers may be useful later, while the current release also needs reproducible behavior, explicit request controls, and a reviewable trust boundary.
question: Which provider boundary did this project adopt for the initial release?

choices.A: Allow caller-configured HTTPS endpoints and models immediately, with provider-side budgets as the main safety boundary.
choices.B: Define a provider-neutral interface first and require provider-specific adapters behind that shared contract.
choices.C: Hard-code two supported providers so the workflow has redundancy without a general adapter layer.
choices.D: Ship one narrow reviewed provider/model profile first with explicit endpoint and request guards.

scenario: Multiple repositories consume one reusable workflow. Upstream fixes arrive frequently, while production consumers need predictable behavior and a controlled way to receive changes.
question: Which production version-tracking policy did this project adopt?

choices.A: Pin a reviewed immutable commit SHA or reviewed release tag and update it explicitly after review.
choices.B: Track a moving major-version tag and rely on compatibility guarantees within that major line.
choices.C: Let automation update consumers on a fixed schedule after CI succeeds.
choices.D: Track the upstream main branch so fixes propagate immediately without per-consumer pin changes.

scenario: A research project already compares several methodologically distinct semantic backends. New credible backends with partially overlapping methods continue to appear.
question: Which backend-expansion policy did this project adopt for the current phase?

choices.A: Replace the weakest existing backend whenever a stronger new implementation appears.
choices.B: Freeze expansion after distinct methodological coverage and add a backend only for an explicit research gap.
choices.C: Add every credible newly discovered backend so ecosystem coverage remains as complete as practical.
choices.D: Add one new backend on a fixed quarterly cadence regardless of methodological overlap.
